title_tag: 9 Best Concerts in Budapest (2026): Prices Compared
meta_description: Organ concerts in St Stephen's Basilica and St Michael's, Vivaldi at St Anna, the Opera House tour and folk dinner shows compared on price, seats and programme.
h1_main: 9 Best Concerts and Shows in Budapest in 2026
author_role: 9 concerts and shows compared on programme, seats, length, price per hour and dinner
lead: The right concert is the one that fits your evening: an organ concert inside St Stephen's Basilica, Vivaldi or Mozart with a string orchestra, a Hungarian folk dance show, with or without dinner, or dinner with live music on the Danube. This page gets you to that seat in under a minute.

To make the choice easy, I compared all 9 on what really decides it: what you actually hear (organ, strings or the full Mozart Requiem), seat categories, length, price per hour and whether dinner is in the price, checked on each seller's own page. Filter by organ, classical, folk, dinner or the Opera House below, or scroll straight to the ranking.

review: This is the default answer to "organ concert in St Stephen's Basilica". For a from-price of €26 you get a full programme in the Basilica nave that builds to Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor, played by organist Teleki Miklós with bass Kolos Kováts and flautist Eleonóra Krusic. That mix of organ, voice and flute keeps it varied for people who are not organ fans.

The difference from the other Basilica series (#6 below) is price and scale. That one starts at €60 and lets you choose between a Mozart Requiem and an organ programme; this one is a smaller line-up at less than half the price. If you just want to sit in the Basilica and hear the organ fill it, this is the better buy.

Seating is sold by row: VIP row 1, Category I rows 2–6, Category II rows 7–16, Category III rows 17–26. The nave is long, so if you care about watching the organist and soloists, a middle category is the sensible upgrade; for pure sound, the from-price seats do the job.

items.title: Budapest: Concert on the Oldest Working Organ in the City

pills.label: Oldest working organ
pills.body: Budapest's oldest working organ, in the Baroque St Michael's Church on Váci utca. The organisers describe it as a small instrument, not a huge cathedral organ, and the programme suits it: Bach, Handel, Mozart, Franck.

pills.label: Organ + soprano
pills.body: Miklós Teleki, the series' creative director, who gives about 120 recitals a year, with soprano Zita Szilágyi on vocal dates. Some dates are solo organ or chamber music instead.

pills.label: Screen on the organist
pills.body: a screen shows the organist playing, and there is a short introduction in English and Hungarian plus a printed leaflet.

pills.label: Heated pews
pills.body: free seating. The old pews are heated, the chairs are more comfortable. No seat categories, so arrive early for the front.

items.pick: for organ lovers on a budget, because €23 buys a 65-minute Bach-to-Franck programme on the city's oldest working organ, with a screen so you can watch the organist play
items.skip: if you want the grand scale of the Basilica or monumental organ pieces; this organ is small by design

review: The best price-to-quality ratio on this list. For €23 you get 65 minutes on what the series bills as Budapest's oldest working organ, in the Baroque St Michael's Church on Váci utca. The programme runs from Bach's Prelude and Fugue in G major through Handel, Vivaldi, Mozart, Franck and Caccini's Ave Maria to Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor.

Two small details make it better than the price suggests. A screen shows the organist, so you can watch Miklós Teleki play, and there is a short spoken introduction and a printed leaflet in English. The old pews are heated.

The catch is scale. This is not the Basilica: the organisers say themselves it is not a huge cathedral organ. If you want sheer volume, book #1. If you want an intimate, well-explained concert at the lowest price, book this one. A second ticket for the same church and organist exists at €25; this one is cheaper and has the longer track record.

review: If your travel companion says "I don't really know classical music", this is the one. In one hour the Budapest Classic Orchestra, a violin soloist and a soprano work through the pieces everyone recognises: Vivaldi's Spring and Summer, Pachelbel's Canon, Bach's Air, Mozart's Lacrimosa, an Allegro from Beethoven's 5th.

At €28 it sits between the St Michael's organ concert (€23) and the Basilica organ concert (€26), but it is a different product: strings and voice instead of organ. Against the €60 Matthias Church string concert (#7) it offers a similar greatest-hits format for less than half the price, in a central Pest church rather than on Castle Hill.
Practical points: doors open 15 minutes early, latecomers are let in between pieces, and the venue is wheelchair-accessible. Food, drinks and pets are not allowed inside.

review: The Rajkó Folk Ensemble show is the cheapest way to see Hungarian folk dance done by professionals: from €15 for a 60-minute performance split into two 30-minute halves, in costume, with live music. The ensemble was founded in 1950 and has staged Hungarian folk dance professionally for more than 70 years.

You choose how much food comes with it. The base ticket covers the show and a drink; higher options add soup or a three-course dinner (tarragon poultry soup, chicken paprikash with potato gratin, Somlói sponge cake, or a vegetarian menu you request when booking). The evening runs on a fixed clock from 18:30 to 20:20, so it leaves the rest of the evening free.

Against the Puli & Juhász dinner show (#8), Rajkó gives you a longer dance performance (60 minutes against two 15-minute sets) for much less money, but the dinner is the add-on, not the main event. One real limitation: the cellar on Király utca is not wheelchair-accessible.

review: This is the one to book if the question is "Budapest Opera House tour". A live guide spends 60 minutes inside the Hungarian State Opera, built in 1884 to Miklós Ybl's plans and fully restored in 2022, covering the auditorium frescoes and the grand staircase, and the visit ends with a brief live concert on the staircase landing.

Be clear about what you are buying: a building tour with a musical finale, not a concert. At €33 it is a fair price for the access and the guide, and it pairs well with an evening church concert from the list above. A second Opera tour with mini-concert sells for about €59 with groups capped at 20; this one costs about half and has a far larger following.
Two catches. The Opera can cancel tours during rehearsals (you are offered another date), and the auditorium is sometimes in reduced light. The tour is not suitable for wheelchair users.

review: Puli & Juhász flips the Rajkó formula: here the dinner is the product and the dancing is the garnish. €55 buys a three-course Hungarian meal (goulash in a cauldron, chicken paprikash with dumplings, Somló trifle, or a full vegan menu), a welcome glass of sparkling wine or juice, live folk music through the evening and two 15-minute folklore sets, after which you can join in for a few steps.

Value check: at roughly €27 per hour for two hours with dinner included, it is fair for a sit-down meal in central Budapest. Compared with Rajkó (#4) you get less dancing but a proper dinner as standard; compared with Apostolok (#9) you get folk culture instead of medieval theatre, but drinks are not unlimited.

Know before you go: drinks beyond the welcome glass are extra, and tables seat 4 or 6, so smaller parties may share. The restaurant is on Dob utca in District VII, a short walk from the Jewish Quarter sights; our Jewish Quarter tours guide covers the neighbourhood by day.

guide.h2: Budapest Concerts and Shows Side by Side
guide.html:
Price per hour is the fairest way to compare a one-hour church concert with a two-hour dinner show. The two organ concerts are the cheapest church concerts here at about €21–22 per hour (less if the Basilica programme runs long); the two €60 series charge more than double that for a similar length, and the dinner shows look expensive until you remember the meal is in the price.

Per-hour figures use the from-price and the listed length. Seat upgrades, dinner options and later sittings cost more.

• You want an organ in a famous church: the Basilica organ concert at €26. Bach's Toccata and Fugue in the Basilica is the classic Budapest concert.
  • You want the best value and like to watch the organist: St Michael's at €23, with a screen on the player and heated pews.
  • You are not a classical person but want a lovely hour: Vivaldi at St Anna, €28, orchestra plus soprano.
  • You want Mozart's Requiem: the €60 Basilica series is the only one here that performs it in full. Check your date's programme.
  • You are staying in Buda or want a Castle Hill evening: Matthias Church, €60.
  • You want to see the Opera House: the €33 guided tour with a short live concert.
  • You want Hungarian folk dance: Rajkó from €15 for the longest show, or Puli & Juhász at €55 if dinner matters more than dance time.
  • You want dinner, drinks and a party: Apostolok from €45 with unlimited beer and wine.

Want music on the river instead? Several boats serve dinner with a live band; compare them in our best dinner cruises in Budapest guide.

guide.h2: Practical Tips: Seats, Timing and What Costs Extra
guide.html:
Seats. In the Basilica, rows decide the price: VIP row 1, Category I rows 2–6, Category II rows 7–16, Category III rows 17–26. The sound carries to the back, the view does not. St Michael's has free seating, so arrive early if you want the front. St Anna's doors open 15 minutes before the start.

Comfort and timing. Church concerts run 60–70 minutes, or up to 130 minutes for the Basilica organ concert. St Michael's has heated pews as well as more comfortable chairs. At St Anna, latecomers are let in between pieces; at Apostolok, arrive 10–15 minutes before your sitting.

Access. St Michael's, St Anna, the Basilica series (#6) and Apostolok are listed as wheelchair-accessible. The Opera House tour and the Rajkó cellar show are not.

What costs extra. None of these lists transport or hotel pick-up as included. At the dinner shows, Puli & Juhász charges for drinks after the welcome glass, and Apostolok's unlimited drinks exclude spirits and cocktails.

Plan the evening. St Michael's is on Váci utca and St Anna a few steps from it, so you can walk to dinner afterwards; see our food tours if you want a guided eat first. Matthias Church pairs with a Castle Hill walk at sunset. For more evening ideas, see the best things to do in Budapest.

faqs.q: What is the best organ concert in Budapest?
faqs.a: For most visitors, the organ concert in St Stephen's Basilica from €26: organ, bass and flute, ending with Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor. For the lowest price and a closer view, St Michael's Church on Váci utca plays the city's oldest working organ from €23, with a screen showing the organist.

faqs.q: How much is a concert in St Stephen's Basilica?
faqs.a: Two series play there. The organ concert starts at €26 with four seat categories by row (VIP row 1 to Category III rows 17–26). The other classical series, including Mozart's Requiem on some dates, starts at €60 with four seating classes.

faqs.q: Can I arrive late to a church concert in Budapest?
faqs.a: At St Anna Church, yes: doors open 15 minutes before the start and latecomers are let in between pieces, so you miss one piece, not the concert. For the dinner shows, Apostolok asks you to arrive 10–15 minutes before your sitting, and the Rajkó evening runs to a fixed clock from 18:30.

faqs.q: Can I tour the Budapest Opera House and hear music?
faqs.a: Yes. The 60-minute guided Opera House tour from €33 ends with a brief live concert on the grand staircase landing. Tours run in English, German, French, Italian and Spanish, and can be rescheduled when there are rehearsals.

faqs.q: Where can I see a Hungarian folk dance show in Budapest?
faqs.a: The Rajkó Folk Ensemble performs a 60-minute show on Király utca from €15, with soup or dinner as options. Puli & Juhász on Dob utca serves a 3-course dinner with live folk music and two 15-minute dance sets for €55.

faqs.q: Which concert is best for people who don't know classical music?
faqs.a: Vivaldi's Four Seasons at St Anna Church, €28 for one hour. An orchestra, violin soloist and soprano play the pieces almost everyone recognises: Vivaldi, Pachelbel's Canon, Bach's Air, Beethoven's 5th.

faqs.q: Are there concerts on a Danube cruise?
faqs.a: Yes, several dinner cruises have live music on board. They are compared separately in our dinner cruises guide.

methodology: We compared 9 of Budapest's most popular concerts and shows (six church and Opera House options, three folk and dinner shows) on programme and performers, seat categories, length, price per hour, what is included and access, using live prices for a normal date in November 2026. Where two listings sold the same concert in the same church, we kept the stronger one.
